title: Lawyers oppose ICC reassessment of victims in Rodrigo Duterte drug war case
summary: Drug war victims" lawyers are opposing the recent adjustment by the International Criminal Court (ICC) Registry for assessing victims" participation, saying the approach would impact future…

blocks.text: Drug war victims’ lawyers are opposing the recent adjustment by the International Criminal Court (ICC) Registry for assessing victims’ participation, saying the approach would impact future applications and prejudice victims involved in the proceedings against former President Rodrigo Duterte.

Common Legal Representatives for the Victims (CLRV) Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan, and Paolina Massidda have asked Trial Chamber III to clarify the participatory framework for admitted victims and future applicants in light of the court’s October 9 decision.

That ruling allowed the Office of the Prosecutor to include Incidents 50-56 in its Trial Brief, but rejected Incident 57 because it fell outside the temporal scope of the charged crimes against Duterte.

Following this decision, the Registry asked the chamber for guidance on reassessing the applications of drug war victims, as at least 13 applications – or 16 of 539 victims who will participate in the trial – now appear to fall outside the case’s scope. They are to be assessed by the Victims Participation and Reparations Section (VPRS) as “Group B”, or applications that do not clearly qualify as victims, “unless instructed otherwise”.

In a public redacted filing released on November 17, the CLRVs argued that such an approach would cause participants and victims to lose “their previously recognized procedural status” and rights to participate in the trial, and that neither Pre-Trial Chamber I nor Trial Chamber III has withdrawn the authorization to participate.
The lawyers said some participating victims were “devastated” upon knowing their status might be affected.
“We are talking about lives, about lives lost. We all lost family members. Will that be disregarded?” one victim was quoted by the CLRVs as saying.
Addressing continued participation of drug war victims

The Chamber ruled on October 9 that two categories of victims fall within the scope of the Duterte case, or the “charged period”: (1) victims of murders or attempted murders committed in or around Davao City between 1 November 2011 and 30 June 2016, and (2) victims of murders or attempted murders committed anywhere in the Philippines between 30 June 2016 and 16 March 2019 during his administration’s war on drugs.

Andres, Butuyan, and Massidda argue, however, that the Chamber’s decision “did not address the continued participation of those victims, nor did it expressly vary or revoke [its] earlier authorisation.”

The CLRVs also question the Registry’s proposed approach and interpretation of the charged period, stating that some applications were excluded due to temporal ineligibility and geographic restrictions, with consequences that raise questions.

“Accordingly, insofar as the Registry’s approach is premised on an interpretation that confines the case to the periods associated with the selected illustrative incidents, the CLRVs respectfully invite the Chamber to not adopt that interpretation in light of the Confirmation Decision as a whole and the prior determinations on victims’ participation,” the CLRVs argued.

The lawyers emphasize a “need to clarify the relationship between the count-specific wording and the broader presidential period”, and that resolving these questions should take into account the contexts of victims’ participation.

In determining the scope of victims’ participation, the lawyers suggest that the confirmed allegations “must be read together” with the definition of the charged period, and that the incidents and victims enumerated in the charges “did not constitute an exhaustive account of the criminality” alleged against the former president.

The lawyers cited the Pre-Trial Chamber I’s decision to confirm the charges, saying that it accepted that “further incidents or victims could be identified” as long as they fall within the temporal, geographical, and other factual parameters of the confirmed charges.
They are also asking Trial Chamber III to direct the Registry to continue assessing victim applications using the participation framework established by Pre-Trial Chamber I in January 2026.

The requirements to introduce additional incidents “should not be transposed” when assessing applications under that participation framework, noting that the Registry expects further transmissions of victim applications until the end of the Prosecution’s presentation of evidence.
“The consequences also extend to potential reparations, the scope of which is linked to the crimes for which an accused is ultimately convicted,” they argued.

“Victims previously admitted to participate should therefore retain their status, while future applicants whose circumstances fall within the same framework should be assessed on the same basis and admitted, provided that they satisfy the applicable requirements concerning identity, personal harm and nexus to the case,” the CLRVs said.
Suggestions on Registry’s questions on Group C victims
The CLRVs also noted the Registry’s request for guidance, particularly on several categories of Group C applications–or applicants that it could not determine where to place.

For missing victims, the CLRVs suggest assessing cases in the “documented pattern of abductions” in drug war killings, adding that “the absence of recovered or identified remains should not preclude admission”.

Meanwhile, the CLRVs say the eligibility of indirect victims “should turn on the harm suffered” and its “causal connection to the crime” rather than just considering their pre-existing relationship with the person killed. They also suggest considering indirect victims’ “experience as a whole”, such as hearing or being spatially close to the victim, rather than just visually observing the act of killing.
The CLRVs ask the chamber to recognize their proposed “rebuttable presumption” of “continuing harm” to enable the admission of children born into families after the crime as participating victims.
P-0002’s evidence of “particular importance”

In a separate filing, the CLRVs “fully support” the Office of the Prosecutor's bid to admit the transcribed statements and associated material of witness P-0002, identified as a former Davao City police officer and a member of the Davao Death Squad (DDS).

Andres, Butuyan, and Massidda describe P-0002’s evidence as having “particular importance” in determining Duterte's guilt or innocence, stating that his “position and first-hand knowledge” make his testimony “particularly significant” in the former president’s case.

P-0002’s testimony covers Duterte’s alleged individual criminal responsibility and intent, the contextual elements of crimes against humanity during Duterte’s mayoral period, and charged Incident 1, or the killing of three unidentified alleged drug pushers by DDS members in or around 2013 in San Rafael, Davao City.

Prosecutors said P-0002 provided evidence on the origins, structure, and purpose of the DDS, as well as the scope of what the prosecution calls the “Common Plan” in Davao City and the roles of alleged co-perpetrators.

The lawyers also supported the Prosecution’s invocation of Articles 18(6) and 69(4) to justify its preservation and requested admission of P-0002’s testimony, saying those provide “an independent and sufficient legal basis” given the circumstances under which the evidence was obtained.

The prosecution previously noted that P-0002 is “no longer available”, but its filing redacted the reasons for such. Likewise, the CLRV’s filing stated that P-0002 is “unavailable to testify before the chamber”.

“Moreover, the need to seek measures under article 56 of the Statute could not reasonably have been anticipated, given that P-0002’s evidence had already been obtained and preserved under article 18(6) of the Statute,” the lawyers said.
The CLRVs also stated that the admission of P-0002’s statement “would advance the realisation of the victims’ right to the truth and contribute to the conduct of a fair and expeditious trial.”
Duterte will be tried for three counts of crimes against humanity and will face before Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou on November 30.—LDF, GMA News
